reviewMetadata.sourceLessonFamily: Rational and Radical Expressions and Equations

learnerMaterial.title: Detect Extraneous Solutions
learnerMaterial.subject: mathematics
learnerMaterial.lessonGoal: Explain why radical-equation procedures can create extraneous solutions and verify candidates in the original equation.
successCriteria: I state domain restrictions before solving.
I distinguish implication from equivalence in a squared step.
I test every candidate in the original equation.
keyPoints: Squaring both sides can enlarge the solution set.
Algebraic candidates are not solutions until they satisfy the original equation.
Domain restrictions can reject impossible candidates early.

vocabulary.definition: a value produced by a solving process that does not satisfy the original equation

rows: a = b | a² = b² | no; a may equal −b

sections.title: Worked example: solve, then verify
sections.directions: The full solution includes the candidate check.

steps: Domain: x must be at least 0 because the square root is nonnegative.
Square: x + 6 = x², so x² − x − 6 = 0.

sections.title: Your turn: apply the domain screen

items.prompt: For √(2x − 1) = x − 4, which restriction must hold before solving?

feedback.correct: You accounted for both a defined radicand and a nonnegative right side.
feedback.incorrect: The square root is defined and nonnegative. Require the right side to be nonnegative too.

items.prompt: Solve √(x + 2) = x. Show the candidate equation and test every candidate in the original equation.

feedback.correct: You separated generated candidates from verified solutions.
feedback.incorrect: After solving the squared equation, substitute each candidate into the unsquared original equation.

items.prompt: Explain precisely why the step a = b ⇒ a² = b² cannot always be reversed.

feedback.correct: You identified sign loss and distinguished implication from equivalence.
feedback.incorrect: Find two unequal numbers with equal squares. Use them to test the reverse statement.

sections.title: Reteach: mark the one-way step
sections.body: Use a one-way arrow when you square an equation. At the end, a substitution check decides which candidates return to the original equation.

items.prompt: A candidate makes the left side 5 and the right side −5 in the original equation. What is its status?

feedback.correct: Equal squares did not make the original signed values equal.
feedback.incorrect: The original equation requires equal values, not merely equal squares.

items.prompt: Solve √(3x + 4) = x + 2. State restrictions, generate candidates, and verify the final solution set in the original equation.

feedback.correct: Your restrictions, algebra, and original-equation checks establish the final solution set.
feedback.incorrect: Separate the work into restriction, candidate generation, and original-equation verification.

whatYouLearned: Squaring is not automatically an equivalent transformation.
Domain restrictions screen candidates before or after algebra.
The original equation—not the squared equation—decides the final solution set.
